bracket: [Textbook misprint: this exercise block's item letters run A, B, C, D, E, F, G, I, J, K — the book prints NO item H, so the sequence jumps straight from G to I. Verified on the printed page at magnification; there is no missing question, only a missing letter. The book's own lettering is kept here so that a student comparing this bank against the printed page finds the questions where the book puts them.]

[Textbook misprint: option (b) is printed as \(\mathrm{Fe_2O_3 + 3CO_2 \longrightarrow 2Fe + 3CO_2}\), with carbon DIOXIDE on both sides. The standard reduction of haematite uses carbon MONOXIDE, \(\mathrm{Fe_2O_3 + 3CO \longrightarrow 2Fe + 3CO_2}\), which is a genuine redox reaction (Fe \(+3 \to 0\), C \(+2 \to +4\)); as printed the equation balances neither atoms nor electrons, since iron is reduced with nothing to oxidise. The option is preserved as printed. The answer is unaffected either way: the intended reaction is redox, so option (b) is not the one being asked for, and option (d) — a double displacement in which no oxidation number changes at all — remains the only correct choice.]

[Textbook misprint: the instruction reads "Justify that the following reactions ARE redox reaction", but sub-item (b), \(\mathrm{HF(aq) + OH^{\ominus}(aq) \longrightarrow H_2O}(l) + \mathrm{F^{\ominus}(aq)}\), is NOT a redox reaction — H is \(+1\), O is \(-2\) and F is \(-1\) on both sides, so not one oxidation number changes and there is no oxidant and no reductant to identify. It is a neutralisation. Sub-items (a) and (c) are redox as the instruction claims. The item is preserved as printed and (b) is answered on its own terms below.]

[Textbook note (not an error): the item asks which ONE of the four pairs has its second species in the oxidised state, but TWO of them qualify — (a) \(\mathrm{Mg / Mg^{2\oplus}}\) and (b) \(\mathrm{Cu / Cu^{2\oplus}}\) are each a free metal beside its \(+2\) cation, so in both the second species is the oxidised form. Only (c) and (d), where the second species is an anion, are excluded. Both qualifying pairs are given below rather than choosing arbitrarily between them.]

[Textbook misprint: sub-item (d) is printed with the state symbol \((g)\) on \(\mathrm{Bi(OH)_3}\). Bismuth(III) hydroxide is an insoluble SOLID, and the book itself prints the same species as \(\mathrm{Bi(OH)_3(s)}\) in Q.4 B (b) on the same page. The stem is preserved as printed; the state symbol has no bearing on the balancing, which is unchanged.]

[Textbook note (not an error): part (b) of this worked example uses \(\mathrm{E^0(Ag^{\oplus}/Ag)} = +0.80\) V and \(\mathrm{E^0(Cu^{2\oplus}/Cu)} = +0.34\) V, but NEITHER couple appears in Table 6.1, the standard-electrode-potential table printed on the same page and named by the question's own wording ("By using standard electrode potential table"). Both values are the accepted standard ones and the worked answer is correct; a student working only from Table 6.1 simply cannot reach part (b). Separately, that table's heading is printed as "Standand electrode protentianls of some redox couples" and its first column as "Oxidised form + \(\mathrm{ne^{\ominus}} \longrightarrow\) reduced from" — read as "Standard electrode potentials" and "reduced form".]
